introduction: As the Church's year draws to a close, the readings turn our thoughts to the end of all things and to Christ's coming. Ten young women wait for the bridegroom; five are ready and five are not. Wisdom, the first reading tells us, is close to all who look for her, and Paul comforts us with the hope that the dead in Christ will rise. In this month when we pray for the faithful departed, let us ask for watchful hearts and lamps filled with faith and love.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: We do not know the day or the hour, but we know the One who is coming. Let us pray to him with watchful and hopeful hearts.
intentions: For the Church: that she may keep the lamp of faith burning in every age, and wait with joy for the coming of her Lord. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who seek wisdom and truth, especially students and teachers: that they may find the wisdom that comes from God. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are grieving: that the hope of the resurrection may comfort them, and that they may not grieve like those who have no hope. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who have grown tired in faith or put off returning to God: that the Lord may rekindle their lamps before it is late. Let us pray to the Lord.
For our deceased relatives, friends and benefactors, and for all the faithful departed: that they may enter the wedding feast of the Lamb. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord Jesus, Bridegroom of the Church, keep us awake in faith and generous in love, so that when you come you may find us ready. You live and reign for ever and ever.

reflection.title: Oil that cannot be borrowed
reflection.body:
At a village wedding in Jesus' time, the bridegroom would come at night to bring his bride home, and her companions would go out with lamps to light the procession. In the parable all ten young women are invited, all have lamps, and all fall asleep while they wait. What separates them is one thing: five brought oil, and five did not.

The detail that troubles us is the refusal of the wise to share. Surely that is unkind? But Jesus is not teaching about sharing possessions. He is pointing to something that by its nature cannot be lent: a life of faith built up day by day. Others can pray for us, and they do, but no one can make our own response to God in our place: the prayers we never prayed, the friendship with God we neglected. The oil is our own response to grace, and when the cry goes up at midnight, it is either there or it is not.

This parable is not meant to frighten us into anxiety. The first reading presents Wisdom as someone who goes looking for those who seek her and meets them on their way. Whoever rises early to seek her will find her already sitting at the gate. God is far more eager to fill our lamps than we are to ask.

Paul writes to Christians who were worried about loved ones who had died before Christ's return. Would they miss everything? No, he says: those who have fallen asleep in Jesus will rise, and together we will be with the Lord forever. "Therefore comfort one another with these words." In November the Church keeps that hope close as we pray for our dead.

So the question is simple: what is the oil in my lamp made of? Daily prayer, however brief. The Sunday Eucharist. Confession when we have fallen. Acts of love no one sees. None of these is spectacular, but together they keep a flame alive through the long night, so that when the Bridegroom comes, we can go in with him to the feast.
